title: Learnability and Privacy Vulnerability are Entangled in a Few Critical Weights
claim: Pruning even most weights leaves train and test performance nearly unchanged after fine-tuning, so a persistent generalization gap remains.
layout: 2 side-by-side bar charts, left-to-right, shared sparsity x-axis with Train/Test legend
description: Two grouped bar charts side by side, each with sparsity levels (0, 80, 85, 87.5, 90 %) on the x-axis. Panel (a), labeled 'Accuracy w/ fine-tuning', has dark navy Train bars at 1.00 and teal Test bars near 0.54, which barely change across sparsities. Panel (b), labeled 'CE loss w/ fine-tuning', shows only teal Test bars at about 1.9 to 1.95, rising slightly with sparsity. Train loss bars are essentially zero, so they are not visible. A translucent Train/Test legend box overlaps the lower-left of each plot. The large, stable gap between navy and teal bars is the main thing the eye sees. Captions under each panel are in large serif text.
caption: According to TFO, important weights are pruned over different sparsities. The results are shown on ResNet18 and CIFAR-100
abstract: Prior approaches for membership privacy preservation usually update or retrain all weights in neural networks, which is costly and can lead to unnecessary utility loss or even more serious misalignment in predictions between training data and non-training data. In this work, we observed three insights: i) privacy vulnerability exists in a very small fraction of weights; ii) however, most of those weights also critically impact utility performance; iii) the importance of weights stems from their locations rather than their values. According to these insights, to preserve privacy, we score critical weights, and instead of discarding those neurons, we rewind only the weights for fine-tuning. We show that, through extensive experiments, this mechanism exhibits outperforming resilience in most cases against Membership Inference Attacks while maintaining utility.
